newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Korea First Bank to fight Hanbo trauma.
newsitem.headline: Korea First Bank to fight Hanbo trauma.

text.p: Korea First Bank, prime creditor of the troubled Hanbo Steel Co, has set out a self-rescue scheme aimed at restoring its financial status, badly hurt by the failure of the group and Sammi Steel Co, bank officals said.
"The troubles with the two firms were a serious blow to us because of our heavy exposure to them," said Na Byung-rok, spokesman of the bank.
"We have to give up interest income of about 200 billion won ($224.2 million) this year on loans we extended to them," he added.
He said Hanbo Steel owed 1.07 trillion won to the bank and Sammi Steel 217 billion won.
Hanbo defaulted on payments of bank loans in January after piling up a $5.8 billion debt and Sammi fell in March under liabilities of more than $1.64 billion.
"Our net will likely turn to loss of more than 50 billion won this year from a profit of 6.2 billion won in 1996," said J.H. Kim, deputy director of the bank's international division.
Alarmed by gloomy business prospects, the bank's union agreed to a 10 percent cut in their salaries this year, while executives accepted a 30 percent pay cut.
"About 55 billion won would be saved from this year's payroll," Na said.
The bank said it would sell off real estates and three of its seven subsidiaries, including KFB Securities Co, Korea First Mutual Savings and Finance Co and Korea First Venture Capital Corp.
Officials at the bank said the sell-offs would bring in 350 billion won to 500 billion won if they were successful.
It also plans to slash some 900 jobs by 1999 from its total of 8,200 employees and close down some loss-making branches at home and abroad.
"Our efforts will help us earn profits again next year or in 1999," the bank's governor Ryoo Shee-yul was quoted by spokesman Na as saying.
The bank's 1996 business was also hampered by rising bad loans and losses in stock investment, officials said.
The bank earned 443.4 billion won in operating profits last year, compared with 404.5 billion won in 1995.

But it had to earmark 273.2 billion won in reserve for credit losses last year as its non-performing loans rose due to the collapse of Woosung Construction, which borrowed 264.4 billion won from the bank.
"Of the total loans to Woosung, about half were unsecured," said Kim.
Officials estimated the bank's non-performing loans at 343.9 billion won in 1996.
The bank also reserved 88.7 billion won for losses in its securities investment in 1996 as a result of a slump in the Seoul stock market.
Financial analysts said the bank's restructuring efforts appeared to be only symbolic as the fate of the bank depended on the government.

"The problems of non-performing loans should be much more serious. The bank is unlikely to survive unless the government helps," said Han Sang-choon, an economist at Daewoo Research Institute. (conversion $1 = 892 won)
